analysis.one_liner: Makes illegal robocalls and robotexts a crime, with up to three years in prison for repeat or mass offenders.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the Senate Commerce Committee from May 2021 until the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The DO NOT Call Act would have turned violations of the federal ban on unwanted automated marketing calls and texts into a criminal offense, punishable by up to one year in prison, and up to three years for repeat offenders, mass callers, frauds, or scams that cost victims $5,000 or more. It also doubled the fine for faking caller ID information from $10,000 to $20,000. Today those violations carry only civil fines, which robocall operations often treat as a cost of doing business. The bill was introduced by Senator Cortez Masto with four cosponsors, including Majority Leader Schumer, and was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone with a phone. Americans receive billions of illegal robocalls and robotexts a year, and many are scams aimed at stealing money from people, especially older adults. Making violations a crime with prison time and a larger caller-ID-faking fine is meant to give prosecutors a real stick against operations that shrug off civil fines. Criminal penalties focus on the biggest and worst offenders: repeat violators, callers flooding millions of calls, and scams that cost victims at least $5,000.

how_it_helps.text: Adds criminal penalties — up to one year in prison, a fine, or both — for willfully and knowingly violating the ban on automated telemarketing calls and messages, which today are enforced only through civil fines.

Raises the penalty to up to three years in prison for aggravated cases: repeat offenders, callers sending more than 100,000 calls in a day or 10 million in a year, calls made to further a felony, or calls causing $5,000 or more in losses in a year.
Doubles the fine for knowingly transmitting misleading or inaccurate caller ID information from $10,000 to $20,000, targeting spoofed calls designed to trick people into answering.

analysis.who_pays: Robocallers and illegal telemarketing operations, including scam call centers, would face prison time and higher fines instead of fines they can absorb as a business expense. Legitimate telemarketers who follow the existing rules are unaffected, since the penalties apply only to willful and knowing violations.

drawbacks.text: Criminalizing conduct creates a risk of overreach: the law covers any willful violation of the automated-call rules, not just scams, so a business making good-faith compliance mistakes could in principle face prosecution, though the one-year maximum is at the low end of federal crimes.
Criminal penalties do not return money to scam victims the way civil penalties or restitution can, and prosecutors may still prioritize other cases, so deterrence is not guaranteed.
Aggressive enforcement could raise compliance costs for call centers and marketing firms that rely on high-volume outreach, some of which pass costs to customers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is broad and everyday: fewer scam calls reaching people's phones and a credible threat against operations that currently treat civil fines as overhead. The main costs — risk of prosecution for technical violations and compliance expense — fall on the calling industry and could be reduced with careful enforcement. On balance the bill targeted a widely resented harm with a proportionate penalty structure, reserving the harshest penalties for repeat, mass, and fraudulent callers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never held a markup or vote on it, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Cortez Masto introduced the DO NOT Call Act on May 27, 2021, with Senators Schumer, Hassan, Klobuchar, and Gillibrand as original cosponsors.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day.
The bill had four Senate Democratic cosponsors, but no further action was ever taken on it.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill died in committee without a vote or hearing.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Illegal robocall and scam-call operations are better off, since they continue to face only civil fines that are cheaper than prison time. The committee system also benefited: a bill favored by the Senate Majority Leader was never brought up, with no recorded vote for anyone to answer for.

for.name: Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to add criminal penalties for illegal robocalls and doubled caller-ID fines.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Schumer
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; did not bring it to the Senate floor.

for.name: 4 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Hassan, Klobuchar, Gillibrand, plus one other).

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in May 2021 and never took it up, holding no markup or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No floor vote ever occurred. All five senators involved at introduction were Democrats, and the committee that buried it was controlled by Democrats, so no Republican opposition was ever recorded.

industries.note: Operations that blast illegal automated marketing calls and spoofed caller IDs would face up to three years in prison and doubled caller-ID fines instead of civil penalties they can absorb as a business cost. Their business model depends on reaching people against their will, so their gain is the public's burden.

The bill only penalized willful and knowing violations, so compliant callers were untouched, but high-volume marketers faced a new risk that a compliance mistake could become a criminal matter. Criminal exposure would likely have pushed the industry toward tighter — and more expensive — call screening.
